feedback: If a learner says the missing 90% is destroyed or 'used up', redirect: energy is never destroyed, only transferred — name the exits (heat from respiration, movement, undigested waste) so all 90% is accounted for.

If a learner cannot say why the chain ends, point them back to the running total: in this model, once it has shrunk to ~10 kJ (a thousandth of the starting energy) there is too little left to support another level.
If a learner expects top predators to be most numerous, rebuild from the rule: each level up has about a tenth of the energy, so it can support far less biomass regardless of body size.
activities.intendedInsight: Because only about a tenth of the energy survives each transfer, far less energy — and therefore usually far less living mass — is available at each higher level, which gives the energy pyramid its wide-base/narrow-top shape, makes most biomass pyramids the same shape, and limits chain length. 'Lost' means transferred out as heat/movement/waste, obeying conservation of energy.
learnerActions: Start with a fixed pot of energy (e.g. 10,000 kJ) at the producer level at the wide base.

Move up one level and track what reaches it: roughly 10% passes on while about 90% peels off along labelled streams — heat from respiration, energy burned in movement, energy locked in waste and uneaten parts.
Follow the running total up the levels: 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 kJ, saying the proportion lost each step aloud.
Try to add a fifth or sixth level and notice there is essentially no energy left to support it; state in your own words why food chains are short.
Change the transfer efficiency between 5%, 10% and 20% and describe how the pyramid steepens or flattens and how many levels become possible.
activities.title: Watch the energy leak up the pyramid

feedback: If the learner says energy 'disappears' or is 'used up', insist they name where it goes before continuing.
If the learner explains few foxes by size/strength, redirect to the small share of energy reaching the top level.
If the learner inverts the pyramid, rebuild from the 10% rule level by level.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising where the energy goes and tying predator scarcity to the energy budget distinguishes genuine energy-tracking reasoning from rote recall.
learnerActions: Answer the prompt: 'Only about 10% of the energy at one level reaches the next. When a rabbit eats grass, what happens to the other ~90% of the grass's energy — is it destroyed?'
Name at least two places the missing energy actually goes (heat from respiration, movement, undigested waste).
Explain why a field can feed many rabbits but only a few foxes, using the energy available rather than animal size or strength.
Explain why food chains almost never have more than about five links.
activities.title: Reason it out loud: why can't the chain be longer?

feedback: For the calculation, confirm 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10: each step is a tenth of the level below it; flag any answer that drops by a fixed amount instead of a fixed proportion.
For 'why short', require an energy-availability reason, not a restatement of '10%'.
For the fox/rabbit item, accept only answers grounded in available energy, not body size.
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can apply the ~10% rule quantitatively and explain pyramid shape and chain-length limits, transferring the reasoning to the biomass question.
learnerActions: Given a producer level of 10,000 kJ, calculate how much energy reaches the fourth trophic level by applying ~10% three times (fill-in-the-blank proportional chain: 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 kJ).
Choose and justify why food chains are short in energy terms, rather than just naming the rule.
Put the loss pathways (heat/respiration, movement, waste, uneaten) in the right place at a transfer.
Decide whether you would expect a greater mass of foxes than of rabbits in the same field, and explain in energy terms why this is very unlikely.
activities.title: Check the quantitative reasoning
